title: What is the best ai game engine?
author: Reddit_User_Original
selftext:
I've tried with Godot and Unreal Engine 5.8.

It shreds through implementations in Godot, but the results always feel a bit cheap / low quality.

UE definitely has a much higher potential, but it really struggles with the speed at which it can implement new content, and the results are worse than Godot at the start. Used UE MCP.

All four attempts with Blender MCP and Meshy MCP. The Meshy models are cool but work still needs to be done in blender.

Haven't tried Unity.

I'm most interested in strong integrations that people have figured out to get highly quality results.

comments.author: MarcusBuer
comments.body:
UE is awful for AI, since every asset is a binary, so AI can't just read the file and relies on the MCP.  
I've made a python script to allow AI to read the UASSET graphs directly, both for materials and blueprints, but it can only extract data (useful to convert BP->CPP and materials->HLSL), it can't write new nodes reliably.

I have tried S&Box and despite it being awful as an engine, it is incredible how direct access to assets is important for AI usage.

I think Godot and Unity would be your best bet.

replies.author: cckynv
replies.body:
Kind of, but not exactly from my understanding of it.

https://unity.com/resources/unity-pipeline-cli-technical-walkthrough

They are two separate pieces of software that are installed separately. Only one of the CLI's features needs the pipeline package, and most of the CLI works without it.

To drive the live Editor with Unity commands, you need both. The CLI sends the command and the pipeline package runs it inside the Editor.

I've been building out tools to get good results from AI in unity and listing them on the asset store. I have [one that does animation](https://af.unity.com/sr/camref:1011l5KHFV/pubref:reddit/[p_id:1011l639073]/destination:https%3A%2F%2Fassetstore.unity.com%2Fpackages%2Fslug%2F392426) very well, and I'll have another package for laying out UI well listed soon.

comments.author: Radiant_Mind33
comments.body:
Honestly, the best AI workflow I've found isn't in heavy engines. It's building a custom React + HTML5 Canvas hybrid setup.

The main draw is speed. Engines like UE and Godot have too much boilerplate and complex APIs that LLMs constantly hallucinate on. Plain JS state management mapped directly to a raw Canvas loop is dead simple for AI to reason about, so generating clean math, state logic, and rendering code is almost instantaneous.

The obvious trade-off is that web/canvas games naturally feel a bit cheaper visually and have performance ceilings compared to native engines. But if your goal is rapid prototyping or lean indie iteration, the instant hot-reloading and friction-free AI output beat fighting heavy engine abstractions during early dev.

replies.author: TechgeekOne
replies.body:
One thing to clarify a bit. It's not the boilerplate and the APIs that trip up the LLMs, it's the fact that the engines are very poorly documented and were built for "one human working at human time scales". I've had to resort to code spelunking for weeks in unreal to get an answer to a question far too often over the years. Iteration times have gotten worse over the last 10 years too so it's sort of a double whammy with the big engines, they're slow and opaque to agents.

Right now you're better off rolling your own thing until someone builds a better engine that's agent friendly. I don't believe it's possible to fix Unreal or Unity to work well with agents given how I've seen them evolve over the years. Godot _maybe_ could do it, the code in there looked decent when I dug into it. Their problem is that they have _very_ strong community opinions and whether that aligns with AI usage or not is still an open question last I checked.

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body: I'm building an AI native game engine. The engine itself is Rust, scripting is in a subset of TS. Since you're already speaking about this, what do you think a serious engine like this should have?

replies.author: TechgeekOne
replies.body:
I can just give general conjecture since nobody has built one yet (myself included, I got a ways to go) but this is roughly what I'm seeing, hitting, or know will come up from my past gamedev experience.
- Fast iteration times, like subsecond. AI can code something and be ready to run before you figure out where to put the code, and so far every single engine fails on this one. They're too slow to iterate in even for me at human speeds.
- Asset handling is the big open question, both for generation in the engine's asset workflow and for managing the data when agents get involved. Git worktrees become a non solution when you get to normal game sizes due to them being a flat clone of the repo. Maybe this looks like a variation of multiplayer editing minus the networking part but I honestly have no idea yet. My personal minimum bound is it handles a 300GB project well (before derived data) because that's about how large the last game I shipped was and that was brushing up hard against Unreal's limits.
- Safe languages (Rust is a great pick btw). AI makes mistakes and the cheaper they are or the more you can avoid the better.
- Well documented and sanely structured amusingly enough. I noticed Claude worked a lot better in my own engine than in U
nreal and some of its likely due to me documenting the code like a religious zealot.
- Testable by agents without the editor or hogging the whole system. Harnesses that let you test things in isolation, run test scenarios in a stripped down engine runtime, do rendering off screen, stuff like that. One of my personal favorites I have is a SPIR-V interpreter that lets agents run and debug GPU code on the CPU.

That's roughly everything I can remember right now. Personally I also think a human friendly frontend is also a must so we can see the output and make direct changes since sometimes that's easier than describing in text, but whether that matters in a few years is anyone's guess. I'm going to build one anyway because I wanted it before AI was viable lol.

replies.author: Radiant_Mind33
replies.body:
That’s the exact reason I ended up rolling a custom JS/Canvas setup in VS Code.

People forget Chromium is basically the low-level C++ engine under the hood anyway (V8, Skia, ANGLE translating straight to DirectX/Vulkan). 

An AI agent can digest your entire state loop and math in one pass without getting lost in engine bloat or waiting on compile steps.

replies.author: TechgeekOne
replies.body: Amusingly I don't think most realize that. There's little incentive to dig that deep into a browser's source code unless you're a CS or graphics nerd (guilty as charged) so they probably assume it's magic.
